title: Selvage Session Protocol — the sealed payloads that are JSON, and the vocabulary a refused frame is reported in
description: `selvage/2`'s binary frame is an envelope of bytes, not a JSON frame, and its layout is CANONICAL.md §6.1's; what the envelope carries sealed is either opaque y-protocols bytes or one of these four objects. Valid against PROTOCOL.md §7.1: the room state the host publishes, the closing that ends the room, the holds a connection announces and the session-key announcement a connection makes about itself. None is a session frame — none carries `v` — and each is canonical when it follows CANONICAL.md §2, `listing` in the order §2.7 gives it, with §3's tolerance for a member the receiver does not know. Every object here tolerates a member it does not know, as every schema in this directory does. `refusalReason` is the thing this file fixes that is not a payload: the local report a receiver answers a refused frame with, which no frame carries and which `PROTOCOL.md` §13.2 binds a client to produce.

refusalReason.title: the reason a refused frame is reported in
refusalReason.description: The receiver's local report, and the check order it is read in: CANONICAL.md §6.1's table, whole. A frame is refused for the first of these that applies to it, and PROTOCOL.md §13.2 requires a client to report the reason rather than drop a frame silently. It is a closed *value* rather than a member — no frame carries it, and a receiver tolerates a member it does not know (§3) — so this is the one place in this file where a string an implementation invents is refused. `bad_tag` is the reason a reader would expect and cannot have: the signature covers the ciphertext, so a flipped tag byte reaches a verifier as a signature failure and no conforming receiver can report a tag failure at all (CANONICAL.md §6.1; `docs/studies/peer-corpus.md` §5.4 measured it). `unauthorised_content` is the one reason here that is not a property of the envelope: an authentic frame from a key the host's state gives role `viewer` carrying document content is refused by the peer rules (PROTOCOL.md §13.5). `bad_payload` is the one reason about the plaintext: an authentic frame whose plaintext is not the object its `kind` defines, which no reason about the envelope reaches (CANONICAL.md §6.1 step 8).

sealedIssued.description: The host's edition of a sealed value: the room state's `issued`, and the `issued` a closing carries above every state the host has published. A count, in CANONICAL.md §2.4's form and inside its bound, because the receiver that compares it against the highest it has accepted may be a JavaScript one. It orders the two values the host signs; a frame's `counter` orders the frames one key signs, and the two are different numbers with different jobs (CANONICAL.md §6.1). The first state a host publishes carries `1` and a closing can therefore never carry one: a receiver's mark starts at `0` and a state or a closing that is not above it is refused `stale_issued` (CANONICAL.md §6.1, PROTOCOL.md §7.1).

sealedRole.description: The role the host assigns to a key in the room state: `host`, `guest`, or `viewer`, the role the host denies a peer's edits to. It is `common.json`'s `role` with one more value and a different author — that one is the claim a `selvage/1` connection makes about itself in `session.hello` (`PROTOCOL.md` §9), this one is a fact the host states and signs, and no server seats it. What a receiver does with a key it commits as `viewer` is `PROTOCOL.md` §13.5's: it refuses document content from that peer and reports it `unauthorised_content`, while its SyncStep1 and its awareness are answered and applied.

declaredRole.description: The role a client may declare in its session-key announcement: `guest` or `viewer`, and never `host`. A state names exactly one `host` entry and it is the host's own connection's, so `host` is not a role a peer can declare for itself; a conforming host honours a declaration, and what a role is enforced by is the clients that conform to it (PROTOCOL.md §7.1, §13.5).

sealedPeerKey.description: A peer's public key: the name of its entry in the room state's `peers`, and the value a session-key announcement carries. 32 bytes of Ed25519 in the encoding the invite URL's fragment writes one in — base64url, RFC 4648 §5, unpadded, so exactly 43 characters and no escape in a canonical JSON string (CANONICAL.md §2.3). The key itself and not its 8-byte id: an id is something a receiver derives (SHA-256 of these 32 bytes, first 8) and an id alone verifies nothing, so a state that named one would commit nothing anyone could check.

sealedPeer.description: One seat as the host's state records it, under the peer's public key as the member name. Nothing authoritative here is a value the server supplies: the key is the peer's own and the role is the host's, while `peer_id` is a label the host wrote about a name the server minted, and no rule in either document rests any authority on it (PROTOCOL.md §7.1, §13.4).

peer_id.description: The seat the host believes this key's holder is seated under. It is what a client reads to answer a question about presence — whether the state's `host` entry is seated (PROTOCOL.md §13.8), whether a key's holder has left (§13.7) — and it decides no attribution and no role (§13.4).

roomState.title: the sealed room state
roomState.description: The host's whole statement about a room, published sealed under the frame key with kind 1 and signed by the host key (PROTOCOL.md §7.1). It replaces the receiver's previous state wholesale: a shorter `listing` is a smaller working tree and not a partial update.

listing.description: The host's working tree as it enumerated it: paths, carrying no content, each held to `PROTOCOL.md` §5's path rule and each a candidate rather than a promise of a readable file, exactly as a `selvage/1` grant's `paths` is. Written ascending by UTF-16 code unit (CANONICAL.md §2.7), which is the only order `selvage/2` promises.

peers.description: The roster the host seats, **by public key**, the host's own entry included: the role each key is given and the seat the host believes it is held at. Keyed by the key rather than by `peer_id`, because `peer_id` is the server's word and a role bound to it would be a role any peer could claim by claiming the name (PROTOCOL.md §13.4). An object rather than `room.joined`'s array of the same name, because this one is looked up by key and not listed. One key cannot appear under two names, so the two errors left are one `peer_id` under two keys and two `host` roles: a receiver reads the entry whose key comes first in UTF-16 code-unit order, so two conforming receivers read one state the same way (CANONICAL.md §6.1).

roomClosing.title: the sealed closing
roomClosing.description: The host's statement that a room is over, published sealed under the frame key with kind 2 and signed by the host key (PROTOCOL.md §7.1). One member is a constant and the other is what makes a replay of an old closing a drop rather than an end: a closing is ordered by `issued`, above every state the host has published.

closing.description: Constant. The kind is already what makes this a closing; the member is what a reader of the plaintext sees, and what keeps the payload an object rather than an empty one.

roomHolds.title: the sealed holds
roomHolds.description: The paths one connection keeps open, published sealed under the frame key with kind 3 and signed by that connection's session key (PROTOCOL.md §7.1, §13.7). It is a peer's own statement about itself, so no member here names the peer it is about: the sender is the key that signed the frame, and a receiver attributes the set by the verification it already made (`CANONICAL.md` §6.1). The set is leased rather than held by the server, which relays it and reads nothing in it.

holds.description: The set of paths the sender holds open, replaced wholesale by the next holds message under the same key. A set, so no order is promised (`CANONICAL.md` §2.7), and each path is held to `PROTOCOL.md` §5's rule as a listing's is; a receiver refuses a blank or control-carrying path rather than the message, exactly as `PROTOCOL.md` §13.3 refuses one in a listing.

sessionAnnouncement.title: the sealed session-key announcement
sessionAnnouncement.description: The one thing that makes a peer's key knowable to the room: a `kind = 4` frame, sealed under the frame key and **signed by the very key it announces**, which is why a receiver verifies a frame of this kind against the value inside it rather than against a key it already holds (PROTOCOL.md §7.1, §13.1; CANONICAL.md §6.1's order for this kind). It is the only binary frame a client may send before a room state commits its key.

key.description: The announcing connection's session public key, and the key that signed the frame: the envelope's `key_id` must be its 8-byte id, and the signature must verify against it. Nothing binds it to a `peer_id`, which is the point — a claim about a server-assigned name is a claim any peer could make about another's.

role.description: The role the sender believes it has been given. Optional, and the one statement about a peer's role that comes from the peer's own key; a conforming host honours it (PROTOCOL.md §7.1).
